claims.text: Equimolar WTaTiVZr has enhanced plastic strain relative to pure tungsten under high-temperature plasma-facing conditions.
Equimolar WTaTiVZr has enhanced toughness relative to pure tungsten under high-temperature plasma-facing conditions.
Processing creates a dual-phase microstructure in equimolar WTaTiVZr.
Elemental segregation promotes the formation of fine secondary phases in WTaTiVZr.
The proposed secondary phases are ductile and enriched in Ti and Zr.
The Ti/Zr-rich secondary phases occur at grain boundaries and within grains.
The secondary phases increase dislocation mobility or activity.
The secondary phases promote crack deflection or blunting.
Increased dislocation activity and crack deflection or blunting enhance plasticity and toughness.
Commercially produced pure tungsten has a predominantly single-phase, brittle microstructure that lacks the proposed secondary-phase features.
Commercially used pure tungsten suffers from limited ductility and low toughness at high temperatures.
At temperatures above approximately 1000 degrees Celsius, WTaTiVZr will exhibit greater plastic strain before failure than pure tungsten under otherwise identical conditions.
At temperatures above approximately 1000 degrees Celsius, WTaTiVZr will exhibit greater fracture toughness than pure tungsten under otherwise identical conditions.
Matching grain size, processing history, and environmental conditions permits the effects of alloying and microstructural differences to be isolated.
Changes in processing or impurities could alter the secondary-phase microstructure and limit the proposed mechanism.
SEM and TEM can be used to test for the presence, distribution, and volume fraction of the proposed secondary phases while tensile and fracture tests measure the corresponding mechanical outcomes.
